Beit Yosef of Rabbi Joseph Karo

date.note: Joseph Karo (1488-1575) worked on the Beit Yosef over some twenty years, beginning in the late 1520s (Adrianople) and largely completing it at Safed; the four parts were first printed between 1550 and 1559 (Venice and Sabbioneta). It is a running commentary on the Arbaah Turim (the Tur) of Jacob ben Asher and follows the Tur's fourfold division into Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, and Choshen Mishpat. The year given is an approximate marker for the first printing of the work, not a precise composition date. The Beit Yosef is openly available in Hebrew on Sefaria (Halakhah, Tur, Commentary).

summary: The Beit Yosef ('House of Joseph') is the vast halakhic commentary of Joseph Karo on the Arbaah Turim (the Tur) of Jacob ben Asher, in which Karo traced each law back through the Talmud and the later authorities and argued his rulings at length. Out of it he later distilled his concise code, the Shulchan Aruch; in the reception of the tradition the Beit Yosef is regarded as one of the great works of halakhic analysis.
description:
The Beit Yosef ('House of Joseph') is the comprehensive halakhic commentary composed by Joseph Karo (1488-1575) on the Arbaah Turim (the Tur), the fourfold code of Jacob ben Asher. Karo built his work upon the Tur rather than as a freestanding treatise, following its division into four parts, Orach Chayim, Yoreh Deah, Even ha-Ezer, and Choshen Mishpat, and taking each of its rulings in turn. The account below presents the work's method, structure, and standing as attributed features of the text and of its reception in the tradition, not as claims the editor affirms.

Karo states his purpose in the introduction to the work. Surveying the halakhic literature of his day, he laments that the multiplication of books had produced 'great doubt and confusion' (safek u-mevukhah rabbah), one author repeating or contradicting another, rulings cited plainly as though undisputed where in fact the great authorities were divided; the Torah, he writes in the language of Isaiah 29:14, had come to seem 'like countless Torahs'. His remedy was a single work that would set out every practical law together with its roots and sources in the Talmud and 'all the differing views of the decisors, not one omitted'. He chose to attach this commentary to Jacob ben Asher's Tur, he explains, rather than to Maimonides' code, because the Tur 'includes most of the opinions of the decisors', whereas Maimonides gives only a single view.

The method Karo describes, and carries out, is to take each ruling of the Tur and trace it to its source: whether it rests on a mishnah, a baraita, a tosefta, or a statement in the Babylonian or Jerusalem Talmud; whether the matter is agreed or is a dispute among the tannaim or amoraim; on what ground the Tur's author ruled as he did; and, where opinions were omitted, to supply them and their reasoning. The work thus assembles before the reader, for each law, the talmudic source with the discussions of the commentators and the rulings of the major decisors, from Alfasi, Maimonides, and Asher ben Yehiel through a long list of later authorities. For deciding the law among the conflicting views, Karo announces in the introduction the rule he will generally follow: the three 'pillars of instruction on which the House of Israel leans in their rulings' are Isaac Alfasi (the Rif), Maimonides (the Rambam), and Asher ben Yehiel (the Rosh), and 'where two of them agree on one view, we rule the law according to them', save where the sages of Israel or the majority hold otherwise and custom has spread against it.

From this vast analytical work Karo afterward distilled his concise practical code, the Shulchan Aruch ('The Set Table'), which states in brief the rulings that the Beit Yosef establishes at length. In the reception of the tradition the Beit Yosef is regarded as one of the major works of halakhic analysis, a standing this entry describes as the position the work holds within the tradition rather than adjudicating it, and Karo himself came to be known by its name, 'the Beit Yosef', after it.
editorial_notes: This entry presents the Beit Yosef on Judaism's own terms as Joseph Karo's comprehensive halakhic commentary on the Arbaah Turim (the Tur) of Jacob ben Asher, and closes the dangling reference from the shulchan-aruch work entry, which names the Beit Yosef as the larger work Karo distilled into the Shulchan Aruch (neutrality #1, #4, #6). NEUTRALITY: the work's method (following the majority of the three pillars Alfasi, Maimonides, and Asher), its comprehensiveness, and its standing as one of the great works of halakhic analysis are DESCRIBED as attributed features of the text and its reception ('as attributed features', 'regarded as one of the major works', 'the position the work holds within the tradition'), not asserted in the editor's own voice; the code's authority and the work's greatness are attributed to the tradition's regard, not affirmed by the editor. The Shulchan Aruch is the concise practical code that Karo distilled from the Beit Yosef: where the Beit Yosef sets out the sources and the debate at length, the Shulchan Aruch states the resulting ruling in brief. The shulchan-aruch work entry EXISTS (data/works/judaism/shulchan-aruch.json) and names the Beit Yosef as its source; this entry closes that dangling reference.
